utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: The court will come to order. I'd like to say good morning to the interpreters, to make sure they are in place.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And to the Defence counsel. Good morning to the accused. First, may I ask you, Mr. Registrar, to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-94-2-A, the Prosecutor versus Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: I don't have ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You don't have sound?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Nor translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Of course. Judge Weinberg de Roca, are you okay? We will proceed. I would now ask for the appearances of the parties. For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Howard Morrison and Tanja Radosavljevic for the Appellant, Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. Senior appeals counsel Mark McKeon for the Prosecution. I am joined and will be joined on the argument by Appeals counsel Susan Lamb and Steffen Wirth, and we're also joined at our counsel table by our case manager, Lourdes Galicia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McKeon. I would now like to explain how we're going to proceed during this hearing. As the registrar announced, the case on our agenda is Prosecutor versus Dragan Nikolic. This is an appeal from the sentencing judgement rendered by the Trial Chamber on 18 December 2003. At the plea hearing held on 4 September 2003, Mr. Nikolic pleaded guilty to counts arising out of events that took place in the Susica camp near Vlasenica, in eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina. Based on the confidential joint plea agreement submission filed by the parties, the Trial Chamber entered a single conviction against Mr. Nikolic for count 1 of the indictment, persecution as a crime against humanity. That conviction incorporated count 2, murder as a crime against humanity; count 3, rape as a crime against humanity; and count 4, torture as a crime against humanity. The Chamber sentenced Mr. Nikolic to 23 years' imprisonment. Are you all right, Judge Pocar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I'm all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic has appealed. This morning we will hear arguments from both parties, but before giving the floor to counsel, I will summarise briefly the grounds of the Defence appeal stated in their written submissions. Mr. Nikolic states seven grounds of appeal. The first is that the Trial Chamber set an excessively high starting point for imprisonment, and that his sentence was not commensurate with sentences rendered by the International Tribunal in similar cases. The second ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber erred in its assessment of the aggravating factors. He specifically challenges three of the Trial Chamber's aggravated facts or findings. In his third ground of appeal, Mr. Nikolic argues that the Trial Chamber gave insufficient weight to certain mitigating factors, including his guilty plea, remorse, and cooperation with the Prosecution. He also contends that the Trial Chamber erred in stating that individual deterrence has no relevance in this case. The fourth ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber failed to take into account, or gave insufficient consideration to, the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia. Fifth, Mr. Nikolic argues that the Trial Chamber erred in declining to apply the principle of lex mitior, which holds that in the event of change in the law applicable to a given case prior to a final judgement, the law more favourable to the person being investigated, prosecuted or convicted shall be applied. In the sixth ground of appeal, the Defence asserts that the Trial Chamber did not afford sufficient regard to the parties' mutual recommendation as to the sentence, and that it erroneously took into account the time he would actually serve in prison. Finally, the seventh ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber referred to matters outside the scope of the indictment and the parties' stipulations. I would now like to remind the parties about the standard of review applicable to sentencing appeals. The relevant provisions on sentencings are Articles 23 and 24 of the Statute, and the Rules 100 to 106 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under Article 25 of the Statute, an appeal is not a trial de novo. The role of the Appeals Chamber is limited to correcting errors of law invalidating a decision and errors of fact that have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. Trial Chambers are vested with broad discretion to tailor the penalties to fit the individual circumstances of the accused and the gravity of the crime. In general, the Appeals Chamber will not revise the sentence unless the Trial Chamber has committed a discernible error in exercising its discretion. A Trial Chamber's decision may only be disturbed on appeal if the Appellant shows that the Trial Chamber erred in the weighing process, either by taking into account what it ought not to have considered or by failing to take into account what it ought to have considered. Before we proceed, I would also ask the parties to be precise and clear in their presentation of the grounds of appeal and their responses and replies. Consistent with our Scheduling Order, the Appellant shall have up to 30 minutes to make his oral submission, the Prosecution shall have up to 30 minutes in response to the Appellant's submission, and the Appellant shall have up to 10 minutes to reply to the Prosecution's response. We will now proceed by hearing first from counsel for Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. Your Honours, I'm well aware of the stipulations upon not referring in extenso to the matters that are already before you on paper, and I have no intention of doing so. But I must deviate very slightly from that, to begin with, by adding to the list of authorities one case for Your Honours' consideration concerning commensurateness of sentence. And that's the case of Banovic, which has the reference number IT-02-65/1-S, which was determined before Their Honours, Their Excellencies Judges May and Robinson and Kwan in October of 1993. And I deal with it very shortly because of the time available to me. Mr. Banovic pleaded guilty to, in effect, five murders and 27 counts of grievous bodily harm occasioned during his duties at the Keraterm camp, a camp described in the sentencing judge as brutal, inhumane, and degrading, and of the offences committed by Mr. Banovic being of the utmost gravity. They also mentioned in the sentencing judgement that the relevant significance of the role of the accused was not ultimately decisive the determination of sentence, and at paragraph 49, said that: "The status of the victims of civilians did not necessarily aggravate the offence since the crime of persecution, under Article 5 of the Statute, included the civilian character of the victims as an indispensable legal ingredient." They found as mitigating features substantial cooperation, a guilty plea, genuine remorse, and the fact that the indictee in that case had no previous criminal comment. I pause to make the observation that those fall squarely with the findings and observations in respect of this Appellant. There was a plea recommendation of eight years; there was a sentence of eight years passed in that case. And I note as a matter of perhaps mathematical irony rather than anything else, that the difference between the plea agreement in the current appeal of 15 years and the sentence passed of 23 is eight years, exactly the same sentence that Mr. Banovic got for five murders and 27 counts of grievous bodily harm, one of which was occasioned by shooting somebody in an unfatal way. And I respectfully ask that consideration of that case go into the point of excessively high starting point and the commensurate nature of other sentences. There are several points which may have not been adequately dealt with. One I want to deal with straight away, and that's this: And that's the question of the timing of the plea in this case. There were legal issues in this matter that had to be dealt with. There was a question of law raised as to male captus. Mr. Nikolic was effectively kidnapped from Serbia and brought into Bosnia, where he was handed over to SFOR. It has been determined that there was nothing unlawful in that by both the Trial Chamber and subsequently the Appeals Chamber. But all that took 18 months to do. The initial finding by the Appeals Chamber took from October of 2001 to October of 2002, the initial determination of the motion by the Defence. It wasn't until June of 2003 that all of the legal issues that, in our respectful submission, were necessary to be determined and aired in this case had, in fact, gone through both the first instance and Appellant procedures. So by June 2003, the legal issues had been dealt with. There has, as Your Honours know, also been considerable variation and negotiations as to the nature and scope of the indictment. This is an indictment which started with 80 counts and ended up with eight as a result of a considerable degree of cooperation between the parties. In June of 2003, the negotiations between the Appellant and the Office of the Prosecutor began. It was not until September of 2003 that those negotiations, which were closely -- not contested but closely negotiated, came to fruition, and that there was an agreement between the parties for the 15 years. That was a position that was taken, and I can say and it's apparent from -- and it must be apparent from the notes of any minutes held by the OTP, that was the position taken by the Appellant from June of 2003. But it took four months before eventually the Office of the Prosecutor determined, through their own observations and analysis of the case, that that was an appropriate recommendation. As soon as that had been done, the then Trial Chamber was appraised of the situation and a guilty plea was entered at the first available opportunity afterwards. So although there was a delay in the plea from the arrest of this Appellant until the date the plea was entered, none of it, with great respect, falls upon his shoulders as culpability. Matters of law had to be aired; he had to be advised as to the matters of law. If there is any fault, then it falls squarely upon my shoulders, as his legal advisor, in telling him that before there was any question of plea, there were areas of law which simply had to be explored which might otherwise have vitiated his guilt in any event. But there we have it. That was a position aired before the Office of the Prosecutor. And at a meeting on the 2nd of September of 2003, Michael Johnson, the then head of prosecutions, said in my presence and in front of His Excellency Judge Schomburg the Prosecution accepted that any delay was either occasioned by the question of the necessity of determining legal matters, or the delay inherent in accepting the plea agreement. And we are grateful for that. The position is this, as far as the Appellant is concerned: We, of course, rely upon and adopt all of the matters contained in the appeal brief, and indeed the response to the respondent's appeal brief. And I don't seek to deal with those as a matter of law or fact, because I've been directed not to do so effectively by the Scheduling Order, and it would be repetitious to do so. I'm going to use the remainder of the time that I have in the first half hour really asking a number of rhetorical questions, which I hope will find favour with the Appeal Chamber when considering the issues that overlie every case in this Tribunal, and they are issues of fairness and natural justice. Because whatever else happens in a court of law, if at the end of the day everybody leaves the court or the room or the Tribunal thinking to themselves, That was fair, that complied with natural justice, that's what law and courts are all about, then all well and good. But if any reasonable person, including the Prosecution, the Defence, or the Appellant, leaves a courtroom saying to themselves, I am uneasy, I don't think the proceedings were fair, I don't think the rules of natural justice were followed, I don't think in all terms that there has been, as far as I am concerned, the sort of good faith I was expecting. If anybody leaves a courtroom feeling like that, then it is a matter that should, of course, be of concern to all of us. And those are the nature of the rhetorical questions that I ask. When it comes to the response to whatever my learned friend for the Prosecution raises --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could I ask you just kindly to stop for a second. Can you hear me, Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I can hear you, but not through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Not through that. I see. I am terribly sorry, Mr. Morrison. We will take the lapse of time into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I explain to Mr. Morrison that I have not missed anything you have said because I have been able to read on the monitor what you have been saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Are you okay now, Judge Shahabuddeen? Mr. Morrison, you may proceed, and I'm sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: The first rhetorical question that I -- I go back. Once my learned friend has finished and, indeed, his companions, then it may be necessary for me to actually respond, but the Appellant himself, as part of the response, has asked that he be heard. I make it perfectly plain that what he says is not something that's been scripted. I do not know what he is going to say. It's going to come from him. He has not asked me to script it; I have not scripted it. And for the last five minutes or so of the time, I anticipate that that will happen. The rhetorical question that I ask is this: What was this Tribunal set up to do. And if we look at the founding documents and the long title, we see it is a Tribunal, and I quote, "to prosecute persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law." We go back to the original Security Council documentation. It may be that my individual submission would be that the ethos would be better described, rather than to prosecute persons responsible but to try persons accused, because that is, in effect, what is happening. And then we turned -- if that's correct, that the object of the exercise is not simply to prosecute persons but to try persons, what's the most satisfactory way that any court or tribunal can achieve its objective. We submit that it is self-evident that the very best that any system of justice can hope for is that persons who've committed crimes and are culpable admit their guilt. If every person who had been indicted before this tribunal, or the sister tribunal in Arusha, where I have also practiced, were to stand up and say, as this Appellant stood up and said, having had the indictment read out in extenso, said, Yes, it's true. I am guilty of those matters. I am sorry for what I did. I can give no explanation for what I did other than badness and madness at that time. But I have come to see that I should plead guilty, I should cooperate with the Tribunal in the future in its work, and I should do my best to reconcile what I have done and indeed the people who've been the victims of what I've done. Now, if every appellant or indictee did that, what a blessing. What a difference it would have made to this Tribunal from the very beginning. What a difference it would have made to the international community, to peace and reconciliation in the former Yugoslavia, and indeed in Rwanda, and how much better we would have advanced the cause of international and natural justice. But not every indictee has done that. They haven't had the moral or physical courage to do it, in some instances; in some instances, no doubt, they are doing it because they are not, in fact, guilty of perhaps any or all of the things for which they are indicted. That may be the case. But look at what this Appellant has done. In the first place, if everyone had done it, the business of this Tribunal, in terms of those arrested, would have long since passed. We wouldn't be looking or worrying about a completion strategy; we'd simply be worrying about arresting some people yet indicted and hopefully getting pleas of guilty from them. In addition to that, many of the victims of crime, especially the relatives of those killed, would be infinitely more at ease with themselves both physically and psychologically, and those damaged lives would perhaps see more hope for the future. That would have the knock-on effect of promoting one of the founding principles of this Tribunal, and indeed of the ICTR, which is that of peace and reconciliation; and if that isn't a worthy objective, then what are we all doing here. But this Appellant could only do what was in his power to do, that is, to enter those pleas and enter them in the somber way in which he did. But what effect can that have? What effect might that have, not simply upon his individual offending but upon other people? If other people look and see that someone has entered into a plea recommendation with the Office of the Prosecutor, has then done all they could by entering guilty pleas, by giving substantial cooperation and by having genuine remorse, and that is reflected in a sentence which is commensurate not only with that recommendation but, of course, with other sentences that have been passed, then that, in my respectful submission, is a very powerful tool and incentive for other people to examine their own position, look inward at their own souls and say, Well, he's had the strength to do it and we've seen the result of doing it; shouldn't we do that ourselves? If only one other person did that, it would be a great achievement. If it fell that that became a habit or a consequence in more than one case, then what a blessing that would be for all of us. It's easy, perhaps, for those of us who are not indicted, not standing in the dock, not going to suffer extensive terms of imprisonment to say, Well, if you're guilty, plead guilty. But it actually takes motivation, as we all know, and as Your Honours' know, not only from your sitting here, but from your sitting as Judges in other jurisdictions, it takes a lot. It takes courage, it takes backbone, it takes an appreciation of natural justice from the appellant's or the indictee's own perspective. Dragan Nikolic, it is said in the documentation that was before the Trial Chamber from one of the experts, Nancy Grosselfinger, and I paraphrase it as this, is more now as he was before these offences than the man he was during those few mad, evil months that he now regrets. There was, and it's been found, genuine remorse, genuine horror - that is my word - but genuine disbelief in what he did and a genuine desire to put things right. He was lost, as he says to me, but now he was found. He has approached this matter since the determination of all the legal matters with what I submit is uberrima fides, utmost good faith. He has put himself effectively in the hands of the Prosecution and thereafter in the hands of the Court. All he asked for and hopes for is the natural justice and fairness with which I started my observations. I have to say, and I'm sorry in a way that I have to say it, but after we reached the accommodation with the Office of the Prosecutor for 15 years and we put in our sentencing brief, we were in receipt of the sentencing brief from the Office of the Prosecutor. That was not a sentencing brief, in my observation and experience, that actually matched the nature of the spirit and agreement which I thought we had gone into the matter, and I was left with a sense of unease and profound disappointment. I do not make those comments with relation to any of the parties who sit across from me now. But I was struck with a sense of unfairness. I do not know exactly what effect that sentencing brief had upon the Trial Chamber, because I'm not privy, of course, to their deliberations. But I was left with this sense that somehow we had taken the hand of justice and shaken it and come away slightly cheated, not by the Trial Chamber but by the system. I make no observations in respect to the learned Judges. It would be wrong; it to be impertinent to do so. I don't. But I can't resist that feeling, because it was a genuine feeling that permeated through me and, I know, permeated through the accused. That's one of the reasons, of course, why anybody appeals. They appeal because of a sense of injustice, and they look for a renewal of the hope of justice. And that's what he's done. That's why we're here today. I urge the sentence of 15 years upon the Appeal Chamber, for all the reasons set out in the Appellant brief, and for this analogy: That the parable of the prodigal son is a powerful parable. A man who returns to the moral fold having departed from it is a man who has to be nurtured, because others look and others follow. And in the business of this Tribunal, that cannot, in my respectful submission, be overestimated. I, on behalf of this Appellant, ask for nothing else than a certainty that, at the end of the day, he has been dealt natural justice. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison, for your argument. I'd like to, if I may, ask you a question. In your written submissions, you asserted that the Trial Chamber failed to set a sentence within a clear and unambiguous pattern of sentencing, and I'm wondering whether, apart from your mention today of the Banovic case, you could point to any particular case or cases with similar circumstances to which your case, the case of Mr. Nikolic, is comparable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, they are set out in the original -- the Appellant's original brief in support of appeal against sentence. A number of cases are set out. Forgive me, I was -- I hadn't dealt with them because I thought I had been enjoined not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: What would be the case that you would recommend that we particularly focus on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, this is a document so well-known to me that I've lost my way around it. Let me just -- if I can refer Your Honours to the original Appellant's brief in support of sentence, the cases that we start to refer to are contained at page 15, really starting at paragraph 32. And we go through a number of cases dealing with the issue, first of all, that life imprisonment was an excessive starting point, and the cases which are dealt with there are principally the cases that have been tried or determined before the Rwanda Tribunal, but not exclusively. And at paragraph 63, for instance, we refer to the case of Stakic; at paragraph 66, Krstic. And then we turn to what is perhaps the question that Your Honour asked more specifically, the sentences after pleas of guilty. They begin at paragraph 4 in the case of the Prosecutor against Momir Nikolic; at paragraph 77, the Prosecutor against Ranko Cesic. That was, in particular, a sentence which we say gives a commensurate sentence. We then go on to the Prosecutor against Deronjic, at paragraph 85, and the Prosecutor against - and forgive my pronunciation - Mrdja, at paragraph 94. And that latter case - and I spell it M-r-d-j-a - is one where we say the sentence was particularly commensurate with the sort of offences -- you're never going to find, we submit, any exact parallels. But when considering what is commensurate, it is a question of getting as near as you can. And if you add that to the case of Banovic, we say that those cases which are contained in the Appellant brief supports the Appellant's contention that the sentence that he got went outside and beyond those sentences that are commensurate with what might be called a mean average of the sort of sentences passed for these sort of offences. I can't say that they are exactly the same number of offences, the same number of murders, the same number of detainees. That's a counsel of perfection; it's never going to happen. But there are plainly commensurate sentences, and we all know that in our domestic -- we all know the importance of that from simply the point of view of fairness in our own domestic jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just One more question of clarification. When in your brief you speak of the principle of proportionality. What do you exactly mean? Proportionality between sentences of different accused persons or between proportionality between circumstances of the crime and the sentence of a particular accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to say I mean it all. Proportionality is a broadly based concept. Again, I don't pretend it is an exact science. That is, with respect, why we have judges and not computers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. I would like to know whether my distinguished colleagues would like to ask any questions. Judge Shahabuddeen, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Morrison --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Morrison, I have benefited greatly from your discussion this morning. One possible area of clarification might be this: You speak of the principles of natural justice not having been attended to as correctly as they might have been in this case. Now, I know that you have expounded this area in your written submissions, but it would help me, possibly also my colleagues on the Bench, if you would be good enough to summarise as briefly as you can the respects in which this principle was violated by the decision of the Trial Chamber in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: In short, Your Honour, and I hope this isn't impertinent, I hope I'm not providing ammunition for a dissenting judgement here, because I know that Your Honour has a very particular intellect, and I mean that as a compliment, without being, in any way, sicut ante. And I'm always worried when you ask me a question in a way that I think that my intellect is being dissected under a microscope in a way which perhaps I wouldn't have felt comfortable with had I not been asked questions by you before. What I mean is simply this: If you look at the totality of the case, here is a man who has committed heinous offences. He's admitted to committing heinous offences. He has come before the Tribunal to do what he can to put matters right. He's done all that he can. He can't do more than to plead guilty, to cooperate, and to have genuine remorse. Anything else is beyond him. What's the other side of the coin? The other side of the coin is this: That having held out the hand of uberrima fides, of utmost good faith, that the Prosecution respond in like terms. If they say 15 years, they should mean 15 years, not, okay, well, it may go beyond that. That's intellectually suspect and dishonest. The Trial Chamber should look at the picture and say, in effect, Here was a man who was represented throughout by counsel, and whose counsel has duties to perform and, I hope, performed them in a way which is commensurate with utmost good faith. The Prosecution have looked at the whole picture, they have come up with a figure, they have looked into it with utmost good faith. This is not a figure of 15 years which has simply be plucked out of the ether. This is a considered figure on all the jurisprudence of this Tribunal which took three or four months to arrive at, in close negotiation. If one looks at it like that and applies that reasoning as a foundation and starting point, then one is well on the way to natural justice. If one departs, either because one is misled or because one takes into account extraneous factors, and I'm not alleging or suggesting malice, far from it, then the principles of natural justice start get circumvented. And once you go downhill from that level playing field, it's very easy for a form of momentum to develop, and arguments to be adopted that in fact support the contention that one ought to depart from the rules of natural justice. I can't put it any higher than that. In a sense, it's an understanding and a feeling that one has when one sees all the facts of the case. You can't necessarily turn to jurisprudence to give you the complete answer; you can't necessarily turn to the facts of the case to give you a complete answer. What one has to do, as I said to the learned president, in the question of proportionality, is to put it all together and see whether at the end of the day there is abiding of unease. If there is an abiding sense of unease, then my submission is that there hasn't been natural justice. If one walks away from the case thinking, Yes, I'm happy with what's happened in this case, and so should everybody else be, even if they're not, then there is a sense of natural justice. It is as much, and I hesitate to use the word, a question of moral philosophy as it is of jurisprudence. I'm sure Your Honour knows what I mean, even if my ability to articulate it is not as it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You have articulated your position nicely, Mr. Morrison. But am I accurate, giving to you my impression of what you have said, that you are pleading natural justice in a general sense, not referring to the violation of any specific rule of natural justice? What I mean is this: You're not contending, are you, that the Prosecution, in fact, violated its undertaking to recommend 15 years. I say that because of something you said to the effect that the Prosecution could not go beyond the 15 years. Did it, in fact, go beyond the 15 years?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: If one sits quietly and reads the Prosecution's sentencing brief, then my submission is that any lawyer of any experience is left with a very distinct impression that the 15 years was mentioned, and then the grounds for going beyond that were set out. I don't put it any higher than that. There is a -- I come from a jurisdiction where there is almost no polarity between the Defence and the Prosecutor. On one day I may be prosecuting a murder; on the next day, I may be defending one. And that's the way it works in my jurisdiction. In the robing room before a case, there is a great deal of cooperation; there is very little animosity, either professional or personal. And so perhaps I am unduly sensitive. I know not. But all I can say is this: It's a bit like the man who's asked to describe an elephant. It's very difficult, but he knows one what he sees one. That's natural justice, as far as I'm concerned. It may be very difficult to describe or to articulate or enumerate what is a breach of natural justice, but you know it when you see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did Judge Schomburg elicit from the accused, the Appellant in this case, that he appreciated that the plea agreement did not bind the Trial Chamber to impose any sentence of 15 years, but that the Trial Chamber could effectively vary from that recommendation? And did your client say that he understood this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. And there is no doubt about that. And had the learned trial judge not said that, of course there would have been something -- that would have been a flaw in the proceedings, had he not done that. The learned Trial Chamber was meticulous in making that observation, and we all understood it. The fact that the Trial Chamber has a discretionary power, however, and articulates the fact that they have that discretionary power is not, of course, a license in itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Morrison, last question: Should I take it that your references to restoration of, what is it, peace and cooperation -- reconciliation takes into account the observations of the Appeals Chamber in the Erdemovic case; that yes, it is true that this sensible entering into a plea agreement would have the effect of encouraging others to come forward with similar pleas and to shorten the work of the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's an inevitable consequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. Your arguments this morning really helped us reflect on certain issues, and I'm grateful to you. We will now turn to the Prosecution. After that, you, Mr. Morrison, will have ten minutes, and as you have suggested, and as indeed is our practice, we'll give a few minutes to Mr. Nikolic to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We are going to perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: 30 minutes. Thank you. The Prosecution is going to approach its argument a bit differently than the Appellant has. We, as the Court reminded us at the beginning, this is not a sentencing de novo, but the question is whether there was a discernible error by the trial court in reaching this sentence. I'll pause for a moment, Your Honour. And the question is not whether -- what sentence this Appeal Chamber would have given the Appellant, but whether the Trial Chamber erred in the sentence that it gave. So I won't respond to most of what Mr. Morrison said this morning in some fashion, because, for example, his observations about guilty pleas we largely agree with, and the value of guilty pleas. I would, however, like to respond briefly to two points that he made before we get into the substance of our argument. First of all, Mr. Morrison referred to the timing of the plea, and I would point out to the Appeals Chamber that there was no penalty given to the Appellant because of the so-called lateness of his guilty plea. In fact, in the judgement, in paragraph 234, they specifically recognised that the lateness, and they put that in quotations, of Dragan Nikolic's guilty plea cannot be considered to his detriment. So although the description of the circumstances on how he pled were not challenging, we do challenge that this had any effect whatsoever on the sentence that he was given. The Trial Chamber, in fact, reflected that it did not. Secondly, Your Honour, I would like to just briefly respond to what I see as an unprecedented attack on the Prosecution and our recommendation at trial for sentencing. Our recommendation before the Trial Chamber was quite clear, that we recommended a sentence of 15 years. We repeated that at the end of the hearing. I think a fair reading of the Prosecution's sentencing brief is that we were not trying to hide the facts from the Trial Chamber of what Mr. Nikolic did. The Trial Chamber ultimately had to impose sentence, and it needed to be informed of both the good and the bad about Mr. Nikolic. And I think the sentencing brief fairly presents the balance that had to be made between the aggravating factors and the mitigating factors of his cooperation. At the end of the day, we supported the sentence of 15 years, and indeed, as you see from our brief on appeal, we have not backed away from that on appeal, and have asserted that we still believe that a sentence of 15 years would have been the most appropriate. The question, however, before the Appeals Chamber now is whether there was an abuse of discretion in reaching a sentence other than 15 years. On those points, I will be assisted in the argument by my colleagues. I will turn the microphone over first to Ms. Lamb, who will address the first three grounds of appeal dealing with aggravating and mitigating factors and the allegedly high starting point in sentencing. She will also address the arguments that counsel made on proportionality and the other cases at the Tribunal. Mr. Steffen Wirth will then address the fourth and fifth grounds of appeals dealing with the alleged error in having insufficient regard to the sentencing practices in the former Yugoslavia and lex mitior. If the Court has any questions about those, although those weren't addressed by my colleague, the Court may indeed have questions. And then I will conclude in addressing the last two grounds of appeal dealing with the Trial Chamber's dealing with the sentencing recommendation of the parties and what they did with that, and the alleged consideration by the Trial Chamber of factual matters outside the scope of the indictment and the agreed facts. With that, Your Honour, and with the Court's pleasure, I will turn the microphone over to my colleague, Ms. Lamb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Lamb, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As Mr. McKeon has indicated, I will be responding to the Appellant's first, second, and third grounds of appeal. Indeed, as mentioned, the fundamental issue in this appeal is whether in sentencing Dragan Nikolic to a 23-year term of imprisonment to which the crimes he pled guilty, did the Trial Chamber abuse its sentencing discretion or otherwise fall into error. As Mr. McKeon has just outlined, both parties at trial sought a sentence of 15 years. However, the Prosecution acknowledges that the issue on appeal is whether, in deciding instead to sentence the Appellant to 23 years' imprisonment, the Trial Chamber committed a discernible error or failed to follow applicable law. Thus the issue is not one of agreement or not with the sentence, however, and while recognising that the Chamber was not bound by the joint submission of the parties, the Prosecution does submit that the Trial Chamber did not sufficiently elaborate the basis for its departure from this joint recommendation. This failure to give reasons, in the Prosecution's submission, makes it difficult to evaluate whether or not appropriate weight was given by the Trial Chamber to the various factors it considered in mitigation. Moreover, the sentence conferred was significantly in excess of that thought to have been warranted by both parties, and it is submitted that the Trial Chamber was in error at least in failing to make the basis for its departure from this joint recommendation more apparent. I reiterate, Your Honour, however, that the Prosecution recognises that the issue on appeal is not one of agreement with the sentence conferred but whether or not the Trial Chamber exceeded its discretionary framework in arriving at that sentence. I will thus turn Your Honours now to address grounds 1 to 3 of this appeal in more detail. Turning to the first ground of appeal, the Prosecution's position is that the Trial Chamber, when alluding to a life sentence in paragraph 214 of the judgement, did not set an excessively high starting point in sentencing. The essence of the Appellant's argument is that a starting point of life imprisonment would somehow have placed the Trial Chamber outside the range of sentences that would have been properly available to a trier of fact confronted with crimes of this magnitude. He further contends that a comparison of the numerical values of sentences received by other accused before this Tribunal is a violation -- reveals a violation of the principle of proportionality. Your Honours, it is the Prosecution's position that the crimes for which the Appellant was sentenced are self-evidently those which a life sentence would have been appropriate. There is nothing in the Statute, the Rules, or the jurisprudence of this Tribunal that expressly lay down a range or scale of sentences applicable to the crimes falling under its jurisdiction. While in practice the weightiest sentences meted out by this Tribunal have generally entailed convictions for genocide, there is nothing to suggest that a life sentence would be inappropriate, at least as a starting point for analysis, where serious violations of international humanitarian law, other than genocide, were entailed. The Prosecution submits to the contrary, that a life sentence is appropriate whenever a certain threshold of gravity of the crime is surpassed. Certainly, this threshold is amply reached in the present case, in which the Appellant has admitted responsibility for nine murders and countless other serious violations of international humanitarian law. The Appellant's crimes, despite their magnitude, may well not be the most serious ever heard before this Tribunal, but this, in our submission, does not render a life sentence inappropriate. Indeed, I would submit that the dilemma for this Tribunal is that once a certain threshold of gravity is surpassed, there is arguably no sentence that is capable of adequately encompassing the enormity of the crimes with which we deal. By way of example, a life sentence would self-evidently be demanded where, in perpetrating genocide, an accused liquidated 900 persons. But the converse would not follow, and hence the killing of nine victims by way of persecution would not compel a reasonable trier of fact to reject a life sentence as an appropriate starting point when calibrating sentence. Further, the imposition of the maximum sanction within the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is not restricted only to the most serious imaginable conduct. This is given succinct legal expression in paragraph 932 of the Stakic Trial Chamber judgement, and it is submitted that there is no compelling reasons for this Chamber to depart from the standard today. I will now turn Your Honours to the issue of the parity principle in sentencing. Although this principle has been recognised in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, it is submitted, Your Honours, that the issue in this appeal is instead how the principle of parity ought to apply in the instant case. The Appeals Chamber has cautioned that the sentencing practice of the Tribunal with regard to cases involving similar circumstances is merely one factor which a Chamber must consider when exercising discretion in imposing a sentence. Moreover, direct comparison of sentences is frequently unhelpful, as ultimately the particular circumstances of each case are unique, and every sentence rendered by this Tribunal is calibrated with the particular case in mind. This, in my submission, is borne out by the example cited by the Appellant which, even if containing similarities to the case of the Appellant, are nevertheless not identical. For example, he has cited the case of Momir Nikolic. In that case, however, the Prosecution requested a sentencing range of 15 to 20 years of imprisonment, which was then ignored by the Trial Chamber which, instead, imposed a sentence of 27 years. He further cites the case of Banovic, who received a sentence of eight years' imprisonment upon a recommendation of the same by the Trial Chamber. Undoubtedly, the facts of the Banovic case and the instant ones bear a superficial similarity, save, perhaps, for some of the obvious features and aggravation with regard to the sadism and gratuitousness of the Appellant's conduct in this case. However, even in this case, Your Honours, one is immediately struck by the Trial Chamber's findings as to the extremely low rank within the hierarchial structure of the camp in question, and the utter lack of influence possessed by Mr. Banovic over detainees. By comparison --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: -- the Appellant in this case is a camp commander whose influence was all-encompassing within his particular sphere. Furthermore, the Appellant has not referenced other somewhat similar cases where the accused received sentences of far greater severity than 23 years. In this regard, I would mention merely the case of Goran Jelisic, a further case which bears superficial similarity to the instant case, but where the accused was given instead a sentence of 40 years of imprisonment. So in consequence, therefore, Your Honours, the only conclusion that is perhaps warranted is that the scale of sentences before this Tribunal is broad. This is precisely because each case is considered on its merits and deserves to be considered individually. Further, the Trial Chamber correctly noted that the linchpin in sentencing is, and must always remain, the individual culpability of the accused, and the crimes to which the Appellant plead were extremely serious, for which the only acceptable response was serious censure. In summary, therefore, the Prosecution submits that a life sentence is not a manifestly excessive starting point in sentencing where the direct commission of persecution, including multiple murder, is entailed. And further, that when considered against the backdrop of the crimes committed, their context, their circumstances, and their consequence, the Prosecution submits that a 23-year sentence, considered in isolation, is not in and of itself manifestly disproportionate when measured against comparable cases before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Lamb, the interpreters would appreciate it if you would go a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will do so, with my apologies to the interpreters. I'll turn now to the second ground of appeal, Your Honours, which concerns alleged errors with regard to treatment given to aggravating factors in this appeal. Your Honours, the Prosecution response is amply set forward in its respondent brief, and I do not wish to add significantly to this response. I wish merely to note that, in finding the Appellant to have enjoyed his offending, the Trial Chamber made factual findings on the basis of the evidence before it. The Trial Chamber correctly acknowledged in paragraph 145 of the judgement that aggravating circumstances must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. The Trial Chamber had no doubt as to the veracity of the testimony upon which its conclusions which principally based. Your Honours, allegations of error of fact on appeal will not result in an independent assessment of evidence or a de novo review of the same, unless that evidence relied upon by the Chamber could not reasonably have been accepted by any rational Tribunal, or where the evaluation of evidence was wholly erroneous. It is submitted that the record in this case demonstrates that the findings made by the Trial Chamber were amply supported by that report. This clearly demonstrates a gratuitous and sadistic quality to the Appellant's acts, and unless the Chamber has any further questions on this issue, I would propose to move on to my next ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Weinberg de Roca?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA
utterances.text: Thank you. What I would like to know is how the Prosecution came to the magic figure of 15 if life imprisonment was considered an adequate starting point?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the perfect juncture, perhaps, to move into my final ground of appeal which addresses directly the Prosecution's agreement with the Appellant that the Trial Chamber committed an error in its calculus of the ultimate sentence, given the presence of significant mitigating factors. Essentially, Your Honours, what appears to have occurred is that, from the starting point of life imprisonment, and despite an acknowledgement that significant factors in mitigation would exist in the -- did exist in the instant case, that there is no clear tabulation of the process by which the ultimate sentence was arrived at. Your Honours, in our submission, we contend that the Trial Chamber did correctly identify relevant issues in mitigation. In particular, the Trial Chamber gave full regard to the guilty plea, which, for the reasons Mr. McKeon noted, is fully adumbrated in the Trial Chamber judgement. Further, it recognised remorse and the other considerations extensively listed therein. In the Prosecution's submission, where the error was occasioned, Your Honours, was in the issue of the weighing of these factors. The Prosecution, in particular, has acknowledged in paragraph 67 to 68 of the -- of our respondent brief that the Chamber failed to provide an adequately reasoned decision as to why a sentence of 23 years was warranted, despite, in particular, the Appellant's substantial cooperation with the Prosecution. The Prosecution's arriving at the figure of 15 years was expressly predicated upon the substantial cooperation of the Appellant. The dilemma both for the Prosecution now and, I submit, for this Chamber also is that, despite its finding that the cooperation of the Appellant was substantial, the Trial Chamber nevertheless failed to adumbrate why the 15-year sentence would, in spite of the existence of significant mitigating factors, have been inappropriate. Your Honour, the impact of the Trial Chamber's failure to fully consider the parties' joint sentencing submission and to give reasons for its departure from it will be addressed more fully by my colleague Mr. McKeon in response to appeal ground 6. Your Honour, should you have no further questions, this concludes my response to the Appellant's first three grounds of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Shahabuddeen, you would like a question now, or at the end of the argument?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: At the end of the argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Because maybe Mr. Wirth will throw some additional light on this. Mr. Wirth?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you have no further questions, I will turn the podium over to Mr. Wirth, who will be addressing grounds 4 and 5. If you have no further questions, perhaps I would grant Mr. Wirth the podium and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Since the question of Judge Shahabuddeen would be addressed to you, I would suggest that he ask you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. I'm in the hands of Judge Meron. Ms. Lamb, we are all familiar with the principle that reasons have to be given for a judgement. But I also seem to recall something in the jurisprudence which says that an appeal is really from the judgement and not from the reasons given for the judgement. How do you reconcile these two principles? I am really searching for some learning from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed. I would submit that the very tension that the Appellant has pointed out, in the Prosecution's submission, perhaps emanates from this very point. On the one hand, the Prosecution fully admits that, upon sentencing, a 15-year sentence was recommended, and that that represented our assessment of the sentence that would have been warranted should substantial cooperation be forthcoming. However, we fully acknowledge that, on appeal, the issue is instead whether, in handing down the sentence it did, that constituted a form of manifest error. The difficulty the Prosecution now has is that we find it difficult to point to an express error on the face of the judgement that would suggest a 23-year sentence was, as such, wholly inappropriate. The difficulty, I would submit, that both this Chamber and we are in is in our failure to understand the reasons that the Trial Chamber employed in departing from that sentence. It may well be that those reasons are proper, and that no error is occasioned. We, however, feel very -- have a degree of difficulty in isolating exactly why a 15-year sentence would have been inappropriate, given the facts in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Should I understand you to mean this: That in the absence of a statement by the Trial Chamber explaining the grounds on which it imposed a 23-year imprisonment sentence, you are submitting to the Appeals Chamber that the only apparent grounds are those which were laid out in entering into the plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fear that in answering -- this, indeed, is a very live question in this appeal. I do fear, however, that in answering it, I would be eclipsing, to a very large extent, the argument of my colleague which is yet to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I don't wish you to do that. May I ask another question: Mr. Morrison can speak for himself when his turn comes, but what is your understanding of his position on the question of the competence of the Appeals Chamber, or the competence of the Tribunal, to impose a life sentence? Did you understand him to be saying that the Tribunal lacks the competence to impose a life sentence, or was it your understanding that he was saying, All right, the Tribunal has that competence but it could not be appropriately exercised in this case?

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Your Honour, to be frank, I am not entirely sure of which -- what basis the Appellant's argument rests. The opening preambular portion of the first ground of appeal does suggest that a starting point of a life sentence would have been per se inappropriate, and our response to, as indicated, that as a matter of law, that submission must surely fail. However, in developing his argument, the argument tends to gravitate more towards the latter of the propositions you have pointed out. And our response would be that as set forth in our brief, firstly; that from that admittedly starting point of sentence, the Trial Chamber fully acknowledged that there were significant factors in mitigation which would warrant a substantial reduction. It is, therefore, in my view, somewhat academic as to whether any form of life sentence was, in fact, every seriously contemplated or imposed, because no such numerical figure was put on such a sentence. Rather, the Trial Chamber proceeded immediately to identifying the sentence of 23 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Lamb, for your response to Judge Shahabuddeen. We will now proceed to Mr. Wirth.

utterances.speaker: MS. LAMB
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will now hand over the podium to my colleague, Mr. Wirth, who will address grounds 4 and 5 of the present appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And may I draw your attention to the time constraints.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for that reminder, indeed. I had prepared more fully submissions, but I will limit myself to two points, in view of the time constraints. Both points concern ground D, or ground 4, as it is numbered in our response. The first observation regards to the Appellant's argument that the Trial Chamber was overly influenced by the sentencing law of other states. As you know, Your Honour, the Trial Chamber gained its information about the sentencing practice of other states from the report of the Max Planck Institute in Freiburg, and in that regard, we would like to point out that, despite the fact that the Trial Chamber clearly intended to refer to the sentencing practice of other states, as it was clear from its request for the sentencing report from the Max Planck Institute, the Appellant never objected to that clear intention of the Trial Chamber. Rather, when Professor Sieber presented the Max Planck report in the trial, the Appellant complimented Professor Sieber for such a powerful piece of research. And it is therefore our submission that any argument that the Trial Chamber should not have considered the sentencing practice of other states has been waived by the Appellant during trial. The second issue with regard to ground D that we would like to point out shortly concerns the starting point of the Appellant's argument. The Appellant's argument that the Trial Chamber erred in not sufficiently considering the sentencing law of the former Yugoslavia, and his starting point upon which his argument rests, is that in the former Yugoslavia, a maximum sentence of 20 years applies for conduct like his conduct. And it is our submission that this starting point is not appropriate. Your Honours, in paragraph 158 of the trial judgement, the Trial Chamber refers to the current Criminal Code of the Republika Srpska, and under this Code, a single aggravated murder is punished not with a minimum sentence of 20 years but with a minimum sentence of 45 years. And as you know, Your Honours, the Appellant is not only responsible for one aggravated murder but for nine cruel killings, and for acts of torture and rape. We therefore submit that the sentencing range of up to 45 years provided for in the current Republika Srpska Code would certainly apply to conduct like his. However, the Prosecution need not only rely on the current law of Republika Srpska. Also, in the previous codes that were in force on the territory, a -- there was never a maximum sentence of 20 years for aggravated murder. Rather, as we know from the Max Planck Institute report, the Criminal Code in force in Republika Srpska between 2000 and 2003 provided for a life sentence, and the old 1997 Code for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina provided for the death penalty. And it is therefore our submission that the competent legislator for the territory of the Republika Srpksa at no time intended that the maximum sentence for aggravated murder should be limited to 20 years. We therefore conclude that the Appellant's argument about the Trial Chamber's consideration of Yugoslav sentencing law should not only fail for the reasons that we set out in our response brief but also because its starting point is manifestly inadequate. Your Honours, I will finish my submissions here with a view to the time constraints, and would be happy to take any questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I think we'll move on to Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I'll sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wirth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm conscious of the time, and I'll try to be very brief. But I would like to respond on ground 6 to Judge Shahabuddeen's question. I think the answer, Your Honour, is that the appeal is from the judgement, but the judgement must tell us whether the Trial Chamber properly exercised its discretion. The Trial Chamber, in reaching a number for a sentence, has to weigh mitigating factors and aggravating factors, and the reason for a reasoned opinion is so that this Chamber knows, in reviewing the judgement, whether that was done properly or not. We do not -- the one point that we agree with counsel for the Defence on and for the Appellant is that in the case, the very limited case we have here, where there has been a guilty plea, where, as part of that agreement for the guilty plea, the Prosecution agreed to recommend a sentence, and the Trial Chamber departs significantly from that recommendation, which in this case is by more than 50 per cent, that in those cases, it's incumbent upon the Trial Chamber to indicate what it did with that recommendation and why it rejected it. This is based on our submission that, in the case of a guilty plea, it is necessary for the Trial Chamber, although it can reject the recommendation of the parties, it must consider it; that it's an important right that an accused gets, to have the Prosecution make a recommendation, and so that it must also be considered; and that the only way the Appeals Chamber can tell whether or not it has been properly considered is by looking at the judgement, and if adequate reasons are not given, then it cannot determine that. And we agree with the Defence that in this case, this particular case, the judgement doesn't do that. In paragraph 281, where the Trial Chamber gave its reasons for the sentence, it essentially said it must weigh the aggravating factors against the mitigating factors. It then discussed in great detail -- well, in two or three sentences, why the aggravating factors were, in its view, made a sentence of 15 years unjust, but it did not address at all why the mitigating factors didn't outweigh that. And that failure is especially noted by us, because our recommendation was primarily, and the most important factor was the cooperation of the Defendant. In fact, our recommendation was conditioned upon his cooperation. And the Trial Chamber earlier in the opinion said that it could not make an independent determination itself of the extent or value of the cooperation, it was relying on the Prosecution for that in finding that it was substantial. So it relied on the Prosecution to find that it was substantial, but then essentially rejected the Prosecution's evaluation of what that meant in terms of it outweighing the gravity of the offence to get to a sentence of 15 years, and didn't give reasons why it did that. Your Honour, briefly, although this reasoned opinion requirement that we urged the Court to have in this area is not found in the Rules, I can't cite to you a Rule that says that this must be the case. I think it's found on the principles that the Rules are based on. First of all, Rule 62 ter gives the Prosecution the right to make a recommendation in sentencing in a guilty plea. Although we make recommendations in other cases, this is the only place where it's specifically stated that the Prosecution can make a recommendation. And I submit that the reason for that is because of the -- of the unique role that our recommendations play in guilty plea cases, where the Defence -- the accused is giving up his right to trial, where there is no trier -- you have not tried the fact. The Trial Chamber has not tried the facts and learned all the facts. The only people that know the facts completely in a guilty plea situation are the two parties. You don't have a trial to learn that. And third, when there are significant mitigating factors, that the Trial Chamber must essentially rely on the Prosecution for. So in order to protect that right of the accused, the Trial Chamber, we submit, must consider that recommendation, and that the only way to know whether or not they have done that properly is to see what is in the judgement, and they must give the reasons, if they reject it, in order -- so this Court can view whether they've abused their discretion, in hearing that recommendation or in rejecting it. I'd also briefly like to address the last grounds of appeal, and again I'm conscious of the time and I'll keep my remarks brief. This was the claimed failure of the Trial Chamber to adequately -- to -- the error in considering factual matters outside the indictment and outside the factual basis, the alleged error. I think this can be considered to be two arguments, and I'm not sure which counsel is making. The first argument is that perhaps the accused or the Appellant was convicted of acts that weren't within the indictment, crimes that he didn't plead guilty to, and therefore they shouldn't have considered evidence of crimes that he didn't plead guilty to. I think the short answer to that is taken by looking at count 1, paragraph 6 of the indictment, which is the persecution count. It describes in great detail that Dragan Nikolic pled guilty to persecution at the Susica camp from early June 1992 until September 1992, and as part of that he participated in creating and maintaining an atmosphere of terror and inhumane conditions. So all of this evidence went to explaining to the Trial Chamber in more detail what it was he had pled guilty to, and those allegations are squarely within the indictment. The second argument he might be making, because in this case the factual basis is the indictment, there was no separate factual basis, is that the Prosecution should not have been putting on evidence before the Trial Chamber that went beyond the factual basis in explaining the acts that he did that he was guilty of. I don't know if this is the argument, but if it is, I think the answer to that is found in Rules 100 and 101, which specifically permit the Prosecution to put on evidence in the case of a guilty plea to explain the sentencing factors, to explain the factors that the Court must consider in exercise its discretion. And I would also note that it did not -- it should not have come to a surprise to the Appellant that we did this, because paragraph V(ii) of the plea agreement specifically permits both parties to submit relevant evidence that will help the Trial Chamber determine an appropriate sentence pursuant to Rule 100. So it's specifically spelled out in the plea agreement that we were going to put on this evidence. It was not improper for the Trial Chamber to consider it. Indeed, it was incumbent upon the Trial Chamber to consider this evidence so that it had a full view of the nature of the Appellant's crimes and what he did, which is the -- one of the key factors that it must consider in sentencing. With that, Your Honour, I would like to open myself to any questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could you please come back to the question of the guilty pleas more particularly. What do you believe should be the impact of a guilty plea on setting the appropriate sentence? We heard arguments of Mr. Morrison on that, pointing out, inter alia, that it's an advantage in avoiding long trials and so on, speeding up the day in court, the arrival of the day in court of the next person, and so on. But more specifically on setting the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't think there's any disagreement by the parties that the Trial Chamber has the discretion to go beyond the plea agreement. That is -- that was, in fact, put into the plea agreement itself, that statement. The Rules of Procedure say this, and as we heard, the Appellant was reminded of the fact that he entered his sentence. However, a Trial Chamber does not have a full view of the facts as it would after a trial, and the parties are in a unique position to evaluate those facts because they know more about the case, in the case of a guilty plea, than does the Trial Chamber. So I think the recommendation of the parties, although it does not bind the Trial Chamber, should be given strong consideration. In this case, I think, Your Honours, this principle is even more apparent because it was a joint recommendation of the parties. So what you have is, not only did the Appellant give up his right to a trial, he also gave up his right to ask for a sentence of less than 15 years. And what you had is you have parties looking at the evidence from both sides and independently coming to the determination, from diametrically opposed viewpoints, that a 15-year sentence was the appropriate one in that case. That is why we submit that it is important for the Trial Chamber to give that recommendation strong consideration, although it's clear in the Rules, and I don't think the parties disagree that the Trial Chamber is, at the end of the day, not bound to follow that recommendation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And would you suggest that the Trial Chamber did not give this recommendation all the consideration that it was due?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, our submission is that we cannot tell from the judgement whether it did that. We're not prepared to say that the sentence of 23 years given in this case was ultimately an abuse of discretion. Our argument, however, is that based on a description that was given of how that decision was reached, it's unclear in the judgement what exactly the Trial Chamber did with the recommendation of 15 years, and whether it gave it adequate weight. So our submission is that the error in the trial judgement is really -- I suppose it's in the nature of a failure to give a reasoned opinion, that the Trial Chamber did not adequately explain the exercise of its discretion. But we're not prepared to say, because we don't have that, that in fact the sentence was an abuse of discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You're not prepared to say that this was an abuse of discretion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that the sentence of 23 years was an abuse of discretion. The error that we do not disagree with counsel on is that there should have been a more full discussion in the judgement on how it reached that sentence. It may well have been an abuse of discretion, but we can't tell from the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would any of my distinguished colleagues -- Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, I caution that no interpretation should be made of any interventions by any member of the Bench. I think we will all accept that. Are you supporting the general thrust of the case put forward by the Appellant that the sentence in this case should be 15 years and not 23?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the Prosecution weighed the evidence ourselves and looked at the aggravating factors weighed against the mitigating factors, our conclusion was, and still is, that a sentence of 15 years is the most appropriate sentence. However, and I hate to add a "however," the judge -- as this Court has pointed out, your role is not to determine de novo what the appropriate sentence is but whether there was an error in the Trial Chamber. And that's also the difficulty we're in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Last question: Am I then right in understanding you to mean that Mr. Morrison was not quite correct in asserting, if I may use the word, that the Prosecution effectively or practically backtracked or resiled in the remainder of its written submissions from its initial recommendation that the sentence should be 15 years?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I see no questions, so I will turn -- thank you very much, Mr. McKeon. I will turn to Mr. Morrison for a 10-minute response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, dealing with just a few matters raised by my -- first of all, my learned colleague, Ms. Lamb. She mentioned the case of Jelisic. Apart from the guilty plea in that case, there were no mitigating features. In particular, there was no cooperation, not indeed a hint of it. The second matter is this: That although the Appellant in this case has been referred to as a camp commander, that is, in fact, an accurate description in one sense, it must be remembered that he was not a camp commander in the sense that he held superior rank over any other guard in the camp. He didn't. No one has ever suggested that he did. He was, in fact, a guard shift commander, so that on the occasions when he was on duty, he was de facto in command of the camp because he was in command of the guards. And on that basis, the description of a camp commander was accepted. But he didn't hold superior rank to anybody else guarding the camp. The third matter that I raise seems to me to be a rather novel proposition of law, that a compliment passed to a professor in court as to the quality of his research waives the right to make any objection to how that research is used, or indeed the overall effect of that. I shall be very careful the next time I make a compliment, particularly if it's too a young lady, because I won't be quite sure what I have waived and why, and nor shall she. I now would ask that the Court give indulgence to the Appellant in this case to address the Court in the manner which he thinks fit and, I hasten to add, not a manner which has, in any sense, been adumbrated by his counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I will now let you address the Court for five minutes or so. If you need a more than five minutes, I will give you a few minutes more. So you may proceed. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I wish to take this opportunity to express once again my sincere remorse and regret for everything I have done. I wish to point out that I sincerely have sympathy for the victims, and I wish to apologise once again to all those I have hurt directly or indirectly. I wish the truth to be known, regardless of what I have done, and I would plead guilty again because not for a single moment have I doubted the correctness of my decision to do so. Therefore, I wish to call upon others who are responsible for everything that has happened in the terrible war that I witnessed to do the same, because I believe that the only road to the truth and to true reconciliation is for everyone to face the truth. I truly wish there to be a process of real reconciliation, because this is the only way forward, the only way into the future. I wish to remind you that it has been more than 10 years since I was indicted. I wandered here and there on my life's road, but no where did I see any future, except on the road that took me out of this labyrinth, and that was facing the truth, however bitter, however painful. I did this, and I believe that I have found the exit from that terrible maze, and that I have thus made a small contribution to the general reconciliation. I hope that my cooperation with the Tribunal will help the victims and their families. I also hope, as I said before, that one day I will be able to meet these people in person, and I will do everything in my power, however small it may be, to help them re-establish a normal life. In my conversation with a lady whose name I don't recall now, a Ms. Grosselfinger, I expressed my wish to contact those people who are potential witnesses in my case, or to write to them. And therefore I wish to call upon all of those who are still looking for their nearest and dearest to contact me through the Tribunal if they fill that I can assist them in this. Let them do so without any fear. I am not asking or expecting that they will love me, but I hope they will contact me. This refers especially to those people whose statements I have had the opportunity to read, and they are quite a number of these, because reading their statements, I realised that many of them do not have real information about their family members who are still missing. I will do everything I can to assist them in finding them, to the best of my ability and as far as I am able to. I would like them not to doubt my sincere intentions. Thank you, Your Honours. That's all I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. You may sit down. Thank you for your statement. And I would like to express my appreciation to the counsel for the Defence, to counsel for the Prosecution, to the interpreters, for their help to the Court in their arguments and statements today. We will now rise. The hearing stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Excuse me. The hearing is not adjourned yet. Mr. Morrison?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: This is just a personal matter. These last few words are the last words I shall say as an advocate in any court, after 28 years of practice, and I just wish to thank this Tribunal, particularly this Appeals Chamber, for their courtesy and erudition in making my last appearance professionally a very happy one. I'm extremely grateful. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Morrison. I appreciate your comments. The hearing stands adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Sentencing Proceedings on Appeal
